episodes.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
episodes.description:
An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter.

The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations.

episodes.title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
episodes.description:
An agent keeps the code changes that improve a language model's score and discards the rest. Weco AI turns that research loop into a workshop, using Mini Parameter Golf to make training experiments small enough to inspect as they run. Zhengyao Jiang introduces autoresearch as repeated proposals and evaluations, and Dixing Xu explains the team's Aiden system and its contributions to OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge. Vayum Arora and Dhruv Srikanth then connect those results to a practical setup that combines a modifiable source file, a fixed evaluation command and a measurable goal.

The walkthrough focuses on what determines whether the search is useful: fast and stable evaluations, a clear direction for the metric, time limits, initial guidance and protection against reward hacking. Weco's experiment tree makes each attempt inspectable, with its code changes and score visible in the dashboard. The presenters show how to branch from promising work and steer a running search toward a different idea instead of simply letting it continue. Internet problems lead to a guided setup demonstration, followed by questions about reinforcement learning and combining multiple objectives. The final exercise swaps model training for a Flappy Bird controller scored across normal play, moving gaps, wind and mixed conditions. A hidden validation set and limits on what the controller can edit make the competition another lesson in designing an evaluation that rewards the behavior you want.

episodes.title: Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal
episodes.description:
An agent can miss an interactive terminal prompt without producing an error. The human sees a question and arrow key options; the agent sees a redraw loop and loses the interface state. PayPal's Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil use that failure to challenge the standard fix of adding more command flags. Flags work when inputs are independent and the path is known in advance. They become awkward when later questions depend on earlier answers or live API responses. Interactive workflows already contain guidance, choices and guardrails that an agent should be able to follow.

The workshop puts that idea into practice with Barista 9000, a coffee ordering CLI that participants adapt for an agent, with a leaderboard and a Mac Mini prize. Patil introduces three approaches: tmux sessions for sending keys and capturing terminal state, IPC side channels that expose structured JSON instead of screen scraping, and context injection that makes options and constraints explicit. Lummus also asks participants to try less expensive models rather than brute force the task with maximum reasoning. Audience solutions push the benchmark toward deterministic parsers and very low response latency, prompting a discussion of what the competition actually rewards. The closing lesson is to keep the CLI predictable while giving the agent enough context and access to navigate its decisions.

episodes.title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab
episodes.description:
A coding agent says it added a duck icon to a podcast page; a browser verification pass checks whether the change actually appeared. That audience demo captures the loop Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora build around two perception agent primitives. Visual annotation lets a person select an element, draw on the page or drop a pin, then export structured feedback for a coding agent. Visual verification checks the rendered site against design expectations and user flows. The annotation step is deterministic and produces JSON; the verification step gives the agent a way to inspect the result of its work.

Arora starts from a podcast landing page whose heading, colors and buttons need changes, then connects the browser extension to a coding agent through a local bridge. Participants modify the extension's permissions and add an Apply Changes button, turning exported feedback into a workflow that edits the code, runs verification and produces a report. Easy and medium paths let them follow the wiring directly or solve more of the integration themselves. A guest demonstration uses a simulated Bee conversation as another source of design feedback, feeding the same edit and verification loop. Audience examples extend the idea to spoken feature discussions, project planning and recorded UI feedback, with several integrations still at the concept stage. The closing discussion keeps the focus on making collaboration visual and checking the rendered result, rather than accepting a coding agent's claim that the change is done.

episodes.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk
episodes.description:
An AI bill of materials turns a repository into a searchable inventory of models, datasets and agents. Javier Garza demonstrates the workflow from a CLI scan to a visual dashboard, then asks it which models the project uses. That inventory anchors a broader security problem: teams cannot assess the AI components they do not know are there. The workshop connects shadow AI to prompt injection, supply chain risk, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency, using Gandalf challenges and malicious instructions embedded in external content to show how an application's intended rules can be bypassed.

Garza works through defenses at several layers. A database view can restrict what an assistant is allowed to retrieve; limited permissions, output validation and human approval constrain what it can do next. Threat modeling maps assets, trust boundaries and possible attacks before deployment, with an intentionally vulnerable student assistant offered for practice. For skills and MCP servers, he separates scanning tool definitions for hidden instructions from scanning the underlying code for vulnerabilities, then explains a scan, fix and rescan loop driven by coding agent rules and hooks. The final sections examine secure prompting, dependency verification, separate development and production environments, IDE configuration and developer review. Governance depends on explaining guardrails as well as enforcing them, because unexplained restrictions invite workarounds. He closes with offensive agent workflows, training resources and challenges that let participants test these ideas themselves.

episodes.title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI
episodes.description:
Open-weight models are good enough now. The question is who can run them fast and reliably.

Yunmo Koo, founding engineer at FriendliAI, argues that open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M3 now compete with the best proprietary models. He shows GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 building similar tower defense games from one prompt, with GLM 5.2 more than 5.6x cheaper. Then he runs the same model and the same coding agent on two providers: FriendliAI builds a Candy Crush-style game in about two minutes, the other takes more than three. He explains where the gap comes from: prefix caching with cache-aware routing and a GPU, CPU and NVMe cache hierarchy for long, repetitive agent inputs, plus hybrid speculative decoding that adapts to live traffic. He also covers why reliability matters for agents (one failed call can sink a whole run) and shares Kilo Code's results of up to 7x faster responses with fewer errors.

In this talk:
• Why open-weight models are now good enough for many workloads
• Why the same model feels different on different providers
• Prefix caching, cache-aware routing and a tiered KV cache
• Hybrid speculative decoding and why reliability is part of speed

episodes.title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
episodes.description:
A tiny Python project contains a hardcoded API key, a SQL injection path and other deliberately planted issues. Killian Carlsen-Phelan runs it through SonarQube, brings the findings into Codex and asks the agent to fix the vulnerable query. The scan follows user controlled input into database execution; the repair replaces string interpolation with a parameterized query. A verification hook checks the edited code again, putting the security feedback inside the coding loop rather than leaving it for a later failed build or review.

The workshop develops Sonar's guide, verify and solve workflow through a live setup of SonarQube Cloud, its CLI, plugin and MCP server. A secrets detection hook blocks a fake credential in a prompt, while an issue listing skill gives the agent evidence from the project dashboard. Context augmentation supplies coding guidance before generation, and agentic analysis checks edits as they happen. The opening OpenAI introduction separates execution containment from artifact correctness and defines completion through a reviewable change and independent evidence. Questions explore how the hooks can be bypassed, which steps run locally or in a container, and which features depend on organizational access. Killian finishes by adding a new database operation under the same verification loop, showing how the setup supports both fixing existing issues and checking new work.

episodes.title: Let Your Agent Cook: Using Skills to Evaluate and Improve Your App — Ankur Duggal, Arize AI
episodes.description:
A financial agent invents answers, repeats tool calls and produces summaries that its own evaluations flag as wrong. Ankur Duggal connects those failures to a coding agent through Arize's CLI and skills, then asks it to investigate traces, change the application and run experiments. The demo begins with an investment question that looks reasonable at the surface but lacks enough context to support its recommendation. Traces reveal the supervisor, specialist agents, model calls and tools underneath that answer. They turn a vague complaint about quality into evidence about the exact steps that failed.

Duggal sets up the CLI profile and skills, then shows the coding agent pulling spans and evaluation results into its local workspace. The investigation uncovers numeric grounding problems, fabricated responses, redundant searches and failures that the agent silently works around. An earlier experiment targets stock queries outside the United States: changing the country context alone is insufficient until the underlying tool is also updated. Dataset, evaluator and experiment skills make those proposed fixes testable rather than a collection of unverified edits. Questions cover local experiment execution, judge models, evaluation costs, sampling and the risk that a coding agent spends its effort on linting instead of the actual defect. The live repair is still running at the close. Duggal recommends human review of proposed changes and evaluations tailored to the application's failures, so later regressions can be detected as traffic and models change.

episodes.title: An AI Future Without the Lock-In — Remy Guercio, Tailscale
episodes.description:
The era of unlimited AI budgets is over, and most teams are locked into whichever tools they picked first.

Remy Guercio, who works on Tailscale's AI gateway Aperture, looks back at a year of AI lock-in and asks how teams get out of it while proving real ROI. He breaks an internal AI deployment into four layers (the models, the data connectors like MCP, CLIs and APIs, the interface, and the sandbox) and argues an AI gateway is what keeps them swappable. He shows how Aperture uses your Tailscale network for identity instead of shared API keys, sets budgets per model (unlimited for cheap models, tight for frontier ones), works as both an LLM and MCP gateway, handles authentication for Cursor, Claude Code and Codex in one place, and keeps logs you can use to diagnose what an agent did.

In this talk:
• Why unlimited AI budgets are ending, and what ROI maxing means
• The four layers of an AI stack and where lock-in hides
• How an AI gateway ties identity, budgets and logs together
• Aperture as both an LLM and MCP gateway

episodes.title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
episodes.description:
Most models learn text first and get vision bolted on later. MiniMax M3 learned both from the very first training step.

Olive, who works on reinforcement learning research at MiniMax, goes inside MiniMax M3, an open-weight model with frontier-level coding and agentic ability, a 1 million token context window and native multimodality. She explains MSA, MiniMax's sparse attention design (about 9x faster prefill and 15x faster decoding than full attention): an index branch that picks which blocks matter and a sparse branch that attends only to those, and why existing designs like DeepSeek's DSA didn't fit grouped-query attention or GPU memory access. Then she covers training with text and vision from step zero, why adding vision later gave unstable results, what the attention maps show, and why 3D attention inside the vision transformer improves visual understanding.

In this talk:
• What makes MiniMax M3 different: agentic coding, 1M context, native multimodal
• How MSA sparse attention works, and why DSA didn't fit
• Block-level retrieval and kernels built for real GPUs
• Why training on text and vision from step zero beats adding vision later
